name: ECU tendinopathy and subluxation
populations: people in repetitive grip and rotation tasks
summary: Pain on the ulnar side of the wrist from the extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU) tendon in its sixth-compartment groove: tendinopathy or tenosynovitis from overload, or subluxation when the ECU subsheath fails.

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: ECU synergy test: sensitivity 73.7% and specificity 85.7% against sonographic ECU abnormalities (40 wrists, one centre); it was proposed to separate extra-articular ECU pain from intra-articular causes

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Dynamic ultrasound shows subluxation, but MRI instability grading did not relate to symptoms in 105 cases, and 6.6% of 755 asymptomatic people had a snapping ECU

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Initial care is usually non-operative (splinting, load management, strengthening). No randomised trial of splinting, injection or surgery was retrieved

keyFacts.label: Injection
keyFacts.value: In a retrospective series of 55 patients, all 11 with an isolated positive synergy test had more than 90% relief after ECU sheath injection, but only 5 stayed pain free

keyFacts.label: Surgery
keyFacts.value: Subsheath reconstruction is described for refractory instability; reviews and small series only, with a continuing debate between anatomical and non-anatomical techniques

keyFacts.label: Associated injury
keyFacts.value: ECU tenosynovitis was more common in patients with TFCC foveal tears than in controls (43% versus 23%)

overview:
The extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU) is the main extensor and ulnar deviator of the wrist [r1]. It runs in the sixth extensor compartment, isolated from the other extensor tendons by its own sheath [r2], and the sixth compartment is only loosely covered by the extensor retinaculum, so at the ulnar head the tendon is held in the ulnar groove by its own retinaculum, the subsheath [r3]. The subsheath is also part of the triangular fibrocartilage complex [r4]. Repetitive loading, or acute trauma, to the flexed, supinated and ulnarly deviated wrist can make the ECU a common source of ulnar-sided wrist pain, and the common pathologies are tendinopathy, tenosynovitis, tendon instability and tendon rupture, which occur in athletes and in patients with inflammatory arthritis [r1].

The diagnostic problem is separating a symptomatic ECU from the many other causes of ulnar-sided wrist pain and from asymptomatic findings. Snapping of the ECU was found in 6.6% of 755 asymptomatic people, with subluxation or dislocation on ultrasound in 2.9% [r5], and MRI grading of ECU instability did not correlate with symptoms [r2]. The ECU synergy test helps to point to the tendon, but its accuracy is only moderate and based on small single-centre studies [r6,r7].

The treatment evidence is limited. Initial treatment is usually non-operative, with splinting, load management, activity modification, strengthening along the kinetic chain and pain management [r8]. Surgery to reconstruct the subsheath is described for refractory instability, with an unresolved debate about anatomical versus non-anatomical methods and a need for comparative studies [r1]. No randomised trial of splinting, injection or surgery was retrieved for this page.

epidemiology.text:
Population incidence figures were not retrieved from the sources used for this page, so none are quoted. ECU tendinopathy and subluxation are listed among the common upper-limb injuries in elite tennis players [r9], and in a series of 28 elite tennis players three clinical patterns were described: acute instability, tendinopathy and rupture [r10]. Ulnar-sided wrist injuries are common in sports that require repeated pronosupination, radial and ulnar deviation, axial loading and gripping of equipment, and ECU pathology is one of the common sources alongside the TFCC and hook of hamate [r8].

Snapping is common without symptoms. In a cross-sectional study of 755 people without wrist complaints (415 women, 340 men), 50 (6.6%) had snapping and 22 (2.9%) had subluxation or dislocation on ultrasound, and all 50 with snapping reported significant repetitive trauma and sports activity [r5]. On MRI of 292 patients with ulnar-sided pain, women had higher subluxation grades [r11]. The ECU and TFCC commonly co-exist: ECU tenosynovitis was more common in 58 patients with TFCC foveal tears than in 120 controls (43% versus 23%), and high-grade subluxation was also more common (26% versus 14%) [r12].

intrinsic: A shallow ulnar groove: a shallower groove was associated with greater ECU subluxation in a cadaver study [r13]
Subsheath insufficiency, including the distal extension of the subsheath, after injury or attrition [r13]
Female sex: women had higher subluxation grades on MRI [r11]
Coexisting TFCC foveal tear or DRUJ translation [r12,r11]
Inflammatory arthritis, in which the sixth compartment is frequently affected [r1,r3]
extrinsic: Sports with repeated pronosupination, ulnar deviation and gripped equipment, for example golf and hockey [r8]
Repetitive loading or acute trauma to the flexed, supinated and ulnarly deviated wrist [r1]
Repetitive technology and hobby use: more than two hours of daily phone, computer or console activity was more common in people with subluxation on ultrasound [r5]

mechanism.summary: In acute instability the ECU is forced out of its groove, and the subsheath is stretched or torn, when the wrist is loaded in flexion, forearm supination and ulnar deviation, for example when a racquet, club or stick hits the ground or a ball at the wrong moment (clinical) [r1,r10]. In a cadaver study the tendon moved ulnarly with forearm supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation, and sectioning the whole subsheath, including its distal extension, caused subluxation [r13]. Tendinopathy and tenosynovitis arise from repetitive loading of the tendon in the same groove, with friction between the sheath and the ulnar groove [r1,r5].
sequence: The athlete grips the racquet, club or stick with a firm hold, and the forearm rotates repeatedly through pronation and supination (clinical; ulnar-sided sports demands [r8]).
The wrist moves into flexion, supination and ulnar deviation, which places the ECU tendon under tension in the ulnar groove [r1,r5].
A shallow groove or a lax subsheath lets the tendon shift ulnarly and palmarly: subluxation increased in supination, flexion and ulnar deviation in cadavers [r13].
A forceful event (a mishit or ground strike) can stretch or tear the subsheath, causing acute instability with a snap (clinical; acute instability described in tennis players [r10]).
Repeated sliding of the tendon against the groove irritates the tendon and sheath, giving tendinopathy or tenosynovitis and localised pain (clinical; friction described by [r5]).
Tenosynovitis may coexist with TFCC foveal tears and DRUJ translation, which can destabilise the ECU further [r12,r11].
Pain increases with pronation and supination against resistance, and the athlete may feel or hear snapping with forearm rotation [r5].

variants.name: Acute ECU instability (subsheath injury)
variants.description: Subluxation or dislocation after a forceful event, with a painful snap; one of three clinical patterns described in elite tennis players [r10].

variants.name: ECU tendinopathy or tenosynovitis
variants.description: Overload of the tendon in its groove with localised pain and swelling; common in athletes and in inflammatory arthritis [r1].

variants.name: Chronic snapping and recurrent subluxation
variants.description: Recurrent subluxation with a shallow groove and an incompetent subsheath; snapping alone can be present without symptoms in 6.6% of people [r5,r13].

variants.name: ECU rupture
variants.description: Rarer; described as a third pattern in tennis players and among the pathologies of the ECU [r10,r1].

variants.name: ECU pathology with TFCC or DRUJ injury
variants.description: Concomitant TFCC disruption and ECU instability are common, and screening for ECU instability in DRUJ instability is advised [r14,r12].

anatomy.text: The ECU lies in the sixth dorsal compartment, isolated from the other tendons by its own sheath [r2]. The compartment is only loosely covered by the extensor retinaculum, and the tendon has its own retinaculum at the ulnar head, the retinaculum privatum or subsheath [r3]. The subsheath, the ECU sheath and the TFCC are anatomically linked: the ECU sheath is part of the TFCC [r4]. The tendon runs in the ulnar groove of the distal ulna; in supination, flexion and ulnar deviation it is tense within the groove and predisposed to subluxation [r5]. The ECU is primarily responsible for wrist extension and ulnar deviation, and it also contributes to the dynamic stability of the wrist and DRUJ [r1,r5]. MRI often shows a centrally increased signal in a normal ECU, caused by fibrovascular tissue, which is a known pitfall [r15].

structures.name: ECU tendon (sixth dorsal compartment)
structures.role: Extends and ulnar-deviates the wrist and acts as a dynamic stabiliser [r1,r5]

structures.name: ECU subsheath (retinaculum privatum)
structures.role: Holds the tendon in the ulnar groove through forearm rotation; its failure allows subluxation [r3,r13]

structures.name: Ulnar groove of the distal ulna
structures.role: The bony channel; a shallow groove is associated with more subluxation [r13]

structures.name: Extensor retinaculum
structures.role: Covers the dorsal compartments, but the sixth compartment is only loosely covered; part of it is used to reconstruct the subsheath [r3,r1]

structures.name: TFCC and DRUJ
structures.role: The subsheath is part of the TFCC, and TFCC foveal tears and DRUJ translation are linked with ECU pathology [r4,r12]

structures.name: Ulnar styloid and fifth metacarpal base
structures.role: Landmarks for palpation (ulnar styloid) and the tendon's insertion (textbook anatomy)

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Two related problems occur at the ECU: a tendon problem and a sheath problem. In tendinopathy and tenosynovitis, repeated loading and friction in the ulnar groove irritate the tendon and its sheath, giving local pain that is greater with pronation and supination against resistance [r5,r1]. In instability, the subsheath fails and the tendon subluxates in forearm supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation; a shallow groove and loss of the distal extension of the subsheath increase subluxation [r13].

The relationship between structural findings and pain is weak. MRI grading of ECU instability did not correlate with symptoms in 105 cases [r2], snapping was found in 6.6% of 755 asymptomatic people [r5], and high-grade subluxation was strongly correlated with tenosynovitis and DRUJ translation in 292 patients with ulnar-sided pain [r11]. A TFCC foveal tear and ECU tenosynovitis are associated [r12]. Because the ECU contributes to the dynamic stability of the wrist and DRUJ, degeneration of the tendon can disrupt DRUJ stability [r5].

structures.name: ECU tendon
structures.effect: Tendinopathy or tenosynovitis from overload; central signal change on MRI can be normal [r1,r15]

structures.name: ECU subsheath
structures.effect: Stretching or tear allows subluxation in supination, flexion and ulnar deviation [r13,r3]

structures.name: Ulnar groove
structures.effect: A shallow groove predisposes to subluxation [r13]

structures.name: TFCC foveal attachment and DRUJ
structures.effect: Associated tears and translation accompany ECU pathology [r12,r11]

structures.name: Sixth-compartment synovium
structures.effect: Tenosynovitis, including in inflammatory arthritis (caput ulnae syndrome) [r3,r1]

muscles.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
muscles.effect: Pain on resisted ulnar deviation and extension; pain-related inhibition reduces loaded ulnar deviation strength (clinical).

muscles.name: Forearm pronators and supinators
muscles.effect: Pain with resisted pronosupination [r5]; compensatory guarding in rotation (clinical).

muscles.name: Grip musculature
muscles.effect: Grip weakens as pain limits loading, and gripped equipment is the main aggravator in sports [r8].

cellular.description: Overload irritates tenocytes and the sheath synovium, with swelling and tenosynovitis (clinical model).
A forceful supination, flexion and ulnar deviation load lets the tendon shift out of its groove (clinical; cadaver kinematics [r13]).
Persistent friction produces tendinopathy, with fibrovascular change that can also look abnormal on MRI in normal tendons [r1,r15].
Recurrent subluxation, snapping and progressive tendon degeneration, which can disrupt wrist and DRUJ stability [r5].

systems.effect: Localised ulnar-sided pain with provocation by loaded rotation; pain processing can amplify symptoms in chronic cases (clinical).
TFCC, DRUJ and ECU share the ulnar-side stabilising role, so treatment of one may need to address the others [r12,r14].
Tenosynovitis can reflect inflammatory arthritis, and the sixth compartment is frequently affected in rheumatic disease [r3,r1].
Racquet, club and stick sports load the ulnar wrist heavily, and grip equipment is hard to modify [r8].

grading.system: Clinical pattern (Montalvan) and MRI subluxation grade (Kim); no validated clinical severity score

grades.description: Subluxation or dislocation of the ECU after a forceful event, with a painful snap [r10].
grades.prognosis: Needs a different approach from tendinopathy; acute cases often respond to immobilisation, and refractory cases need surgery [r10,r16]

grades.description: Overload pain along the tendon in the groove, worse with resisted ulnar deviation and rotation [r10,r1].
Grade 0 no subluxation; grade 1 displacement under 50% of tendon width; grade 2 51–99%; grade 3 100% of tendon width [r11].
grades.prognosis: High-grade subluxation correlated with tenosynovitis and DRUJ translation, but grading did not relate to symptoms in another series [r11,r2]

timeframes.summary: There is no validated healing timeline for ECU tendinopathy or subluxation. The phases below are common clinical conventions based on tendon biology, with the caveat that no trial data were retrieved. Acute cases often respond to immobilisation, and refractory cases need surgery [r16].

healing.description: Relative rest, splinting if needed and avoidance of the flexion, supination and ulnar deviation combination (clinical) [r8]
Pain-free range then isometric loading of the ECU (clinical convention)
Progressive ECU, forearm and grip loading, kinetic chain strengthening [r8]

healing.phase: Return to sport and decision point for refractory cases
healing.description: Graded return to grip and swing sports; persistent snapping or pain despite a well-delivered program may prompt injection or surgical review [r16,r1]

milestones.label: Reassess after 4–6 weeks of protection and load modification
milestones.note: A common clinical convention; no trial data were retrieved

milestones.label: Review of response to a strengthening program
milestones.note: A 3-month trial before discussing injection or surgery is a common clinical convention

milestones.label: Typical return to grip sport in non-operative care

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. A common clinical range after non-operative care is about 6–12 weeks for tendinopathy and longer for subluxation or after subsheath reconstruction, where the surgeon's protocol applies. No trial data were retrieved.

symptoms: Ulnar-sided wrist pain localised over the ECU groove at the ulnar styloid, worse with resisted rotation, gripping and ulnar deviation [r2,r5]
A painful snap or click with forearm rotation, or a feeling of the tendon slipping (instability) [r10]
Gradual onset in racquet, golf or stick sports (tendinopathy), or an acute event with a snap (instability) [r10,r8]
Swelling or tenderness along the tendon and weakness of grip
Pain with loaded wrist extension and ulnar deviation, for example gripping a racquet, club or stick
signs: Tenderness over the ECU tendon in the groove and at the ulnar styloid [r2]
A positive ECU synergy test (pain with the tendon loaded in isolation [r6,r7])
Visible or palpable subluxation or a snap on supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation (clinical; cadaver kinematics [r13])
Swelling or crepitus along the sixth compartment (clinical)
Pain on resisted ulnar deviation and extension and with pronation and supination against resistance [r5]

subjective: Mechanism and sport: acute event versus gradual onset; racquet, club or stick sports and equipment [r10,r8]
Site of pain: over the ulnar groove versus within the wrist or on the dorsal ulnar border
Snapping, clicking or giving way with forearm rotation (instability or TFCC)
Aggravating tasks: resisted rotation, gripping, loaded ulnar deviation and swinging [r8]
Previous wrist injury, TFCC or DRUJ symptoms and previous injections
Inflammatory arthritis, morning stiffness or multiple joint symptoms [r1]
observation: Visible subluxation of the tendon with rotation
palpation: ECU tendon in its groove, between the ulnar styloid and the ulnar head [r2]
Palpate during active supination, flexion and ulnar deviation for a snap [r13]
Ulnar fovea, TFCC and the ulnocarpal joint line for associated pathology [r12]
Hook of hamate, pisiform and triquetrum to separate differentials
rangeOfMotion: Wrist flexion, extension, radial and ulnar deviation
strength: Grip dynamometry compared with the other hand
neuro: Sensation over the dorsal ulnar border of the hand (dorsal ulnar sensory branch)
Ulnar nerve screen if sensory or motor symptoms are present
functional: Observe the racquet, club or stick grip and swing
Sport-specific loaded rotation and ulnar deviation

specialTests.name: ECU synergy test
specialTests.purpose: Load the ECU tendon in isolation to separate ECU tendinopathy from intra-articular ulnar-sided pain
specialTests.procedure: With the forearm supinated, the ECU is fully loaded in isolation by resisted contraction, and the examiner palpates the tendon in its groove. Hand positions beyond 'supination with ECU fully loaded' were not described in the abstracts read, so follow the original description.
specialTests.positive: Pain over the ECU with the test and no pain with the remainder of the examination suggests isolated ECU tendinopathy. Sensitivity and specificity were moderate and the sample was small and single-centre [r7,r6].
specialTests.sensitivity: 73.7% against sonographic ECU abnormality in chronic dorsal ulnar-sided pain

specialTests.name: Carpal supination test
specialTests.purpose: A provocative manoeuvre that loads the ECU compartment
specialTests.procedure: Both the hand and the forearm are supinated (carpal supination), which loaded the sixth compartment in the cadaver study; palpate the ECU groove for pain.
specialTests.positive: Pain over the ECU. In a cadaver study of 9 arms, pressure and strain in the sixth compartment were highest for the carpal supination test, which the authors suggested was the most sensitive test; no clinical accuracy figures were retrieved [r17].

specialTests.name: Subluxation provocation (supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation)
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce subluxation or snapping of the ECU
specialTests.procedure: Palpate or watch the ECU groove while the patient actively supinates the forearm and moves the wrist into flexion and ulnar deviation; compare with the other side. Ultrasound can confirm the displacement.
specialTests.positive: A palpable or visible tendon displacement or snap reproducing symptoms. Because snapping occurs in 6.6% of asymptomatic people, a snap alone does not prove the pain source [r5].

clinicalRules.name: Match findings to symptoms
clinicalRules.description: Snapping was found in 6.6% of 755 asymptomatic people and ECU instability grading on MRI did not relate to symptoms, so the ECU should be treated as the pain source only when palpation, the synergy test and the history agree [r5,r2].

clinicalRules.name: Look for coexisting ulnar-side pathology
clinicalRules.description: ECU tenosynovitis was more common with TFCC foveal tears (43% versus 23%), and TFCC disruption and ECU instability are common concomitant injuries; screen the DRUJ and TFCC in every case [r12,r14].

clinicalRules.name: A positive synergy test can still coexist with intra-articular pathology
clinicalRules.description: In the original series, patients with a positive synergy test and exams suggesting intra-articular pathology often had persistent or recurrent symptoms after ECU sheath injection, and several had ulnocarpal pathology on MRI or arthroscopy [r6].

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE) or QuickDASH
outcomeMeasures.use: Wrist pain and function (clinical use; used for wrist research)

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain VAS or NPRS during grip and swing
outcomeMeasures.use: Activity-specific pain; pain scores were used in subsheath reconstruction series [r18]

outcomeMeasures.name: Grip dynamometry
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective strength compared with the other hand; grip improved from 72% to 93% of the uninjured side after combined TFCC and ECU surgery in a small series [r14]

outcomeMeasures.name: Modified Mayo Wrist Score
outcomeMeasures.use: Used in surgical series of ECU stabilisation; improved from 66.4 to 92.7 in 11 patients [r14,r18]

imaging.indication: Suspected subluxation or snapping; also useful to guide injection
imaging.findings: Shows tendon position relative to the groove during rotation; in a study of 755 people subluxation or dislocation was found in 2.9% of asymptomatic wrists [r5]. Ultrasound was also used as the reference for the synergy test [r7].

imaging.indication: Persisting ulnar-sided pain, associated TFCC or DRUJ injury, or inflammatory arthritis
imaging.findings: Subluxation can be graded 0–3, and high grades correlate with tenosynovitis and DRUJ translation [r11]. MRI instability did not relate to symptoms in 105 cases [r2]. A central high signal in a normal ECU is a pitfall caused by fibrovascular tissue [r15].

imaging.indication: Ulnar-sided pain after trauma, to exclude fracture, DRUJ arthritis and ulnar variance
imaging.findings: Ulnar styloid or hamate fracture, DRUJ arthritis; not diagnostic for the ECU (clinical).

differentials.name: TFCC injury
differentials.distinguishing: Fovea tenderness and pain on loaded rotation or ulnocarpal stress; ECU tenosynovitis commonly coexists with foveal tears [r12].

differentials.name: Hook of hamate fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness over the hook, pain gripping a club or racquet and a positive hook pull test; image with CT.

differentials.name: Ulnar tunnel syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Numbness and weakness in the ulnar nerve distribution with a Tinel sign at Guyon's canal.

differentials.name: Scapholunate ligament injury
differentials.distinguishing: Dorsal-radial pain over the scapholunate interval, not the ulnar groove.

differentials.name: Distal radioulnar joint instability or arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and clunking with forearm rotation, positive DRUJ stress test; ECU instability and DRUJ instability can coexist [r14].

differentials.name: Lunotriquetral ligament injury or pisotriquetral arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness at the lunotriquetral interval or pisiform with a positive shear or grind test (clinical).

differentials.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Palmar-ulnar pain over the FCU insertion at the pisiform, worse with resisted flexion and ulnar deviation (clinical).

differentials.name: Inflammatory arthritis (caput ulnae syndrome)
differentials.distinguishing: Multiple joints, morning stiffness, synovitis of the sixth compartment and systemic features; arrange medical review [r3].

redFlags: Sudden loss of wrist extension or ulnar deviation after a snap or a forceful event: suspect ECU rupture or a major extensor tendon injury and refer to hand surgery [r10].
Hot, red, swollen sixth compartment with fever or a wound near the wrist: suspect infection (septic tenosynovitis); refer to emergency.
Swelling of several joints, morning stiffness longer than 30 minutes or systemic symptoms: suspect inflammatory arthritis (caput ulnae) and arrange medical review [r1,r3].
Trauma with focal bony tenderness over the hook of hamate, triquetrum or ulnar styloid: image for fracture before attributing pain to the tendon.
Persisting pain or recurrent snapping after a well-delivered non-operative program, or DRUJ instability: refer to hand surgery, since TFCC and ECU problems often coexist [r14,r12].
A locked or unstable DRUJ after high-energy trauma: urgent hand surgery review.

management.principles: Treat the patient's pain, not the image. Because snapping and MRI instability can be found without symptoms [r5,r2], the ECU is treated when the history, palpation and synergy test point to it. Initial treatment is usually non-operative, with splinting, load management, activity modification, strengthening along the kinetic chain and pain management [r8]. Acute cases often respond to immobilisation, while refractory cases need surgery [r16]. Montalvan et al. described three patterns in tennis players (acute instability, tendinopathy and rupture) that need different approaches [r10]. No randomised trial of splinting, injection or surgery was retrieved, and the surgical literature consists of reviews and small series with an unresolved debate between anatomical and non-anatomical subsheath reconstruction [r1]. Screen for TFCC and DRUJ pathology, because treating one without the other may leave pain [r14,r12].

medical.name: Splint or immobilisation for acute instability or irritable tendinopathy
medical.description: Acute subsheath injuries often respond to immobilisation, with surgery needed for refractory cases, according to a technique paper's introduction; the splint position and duration are not specified in the abstract [r16]. A common clinical option is a splint holding the wrist and forearm away from supination, flexion and ulnar deviation for several weeks, but no trial data were retrieved.

medical.name: Analgesia and NSAIDs
medical.description: Pain management is part of initial non-operative care in athletes [r8]. No ECU-specific trial of oral or topical NSAIDs was retrieved.

medical.name: Corticosteroid injection of the ECU sheath
medical.description: In a retrospective series of 55 patients with more than 4 months of dorsal ulnar-sided pain, all 11 with an isolated positive synergy test had over 90% pain relief, and 5 stayed pain free. Of 22 with a positive synergy test and signs of intra-articular pathology, 17 had over 90% relief but 10 had recurrent symptoms, 6 with ulnocarpal pathology confirmed. No control group, and injection was used diagnostically. Tendon weakening from corticosteroid near a tendon is a general concern (clinical) [r6].

medical.name: Subsheath reconstruction for refractory instability (anatomical or non-anatomical)
medical.description: A review described the debate between anatomical and non-anatomical techniques, noting that using part of the extensor retinaculum is common and shows successful outcomes, with comparative studies still needed [r1]. In 7 patients offered reconstruction with the dorsal DRUJ capsule after failed conservative care, all but one improved; 4 had excellent Mayo scores, one had an asymptomatic recurrence on ultrasound and 2 needed further surgery [r18].

medical.name: Combined TFCC repair and ECU stabilisation when both are present
medical.description: In 11 patients with DRUJ instability and ECU subluxation who failed therapy, simultaneous open foveal TFCC repair and ECU stabilisation gave pain freedom in 10, grip rising from 72% to 93% and Mayo score from 66.4 to 92.7 at an average 18 months; level IV, no control [r14].

medical.name: Treating an imaging finding of ECU subluxation or instability without matching symptoms
medical.description: Snapping was found in 6.6% of 755 asymptomatic people and MRI instability did not relate to symptoms in 105 cases, so imaging alone should not drive treatment [r5,r2].

physio.name: Education, load management and equipment modification
physio.description: Explain the load-tolerance model, modify grip size, racquet or club handling and swing volume, and avoid the flexion, supination and ulnar deviation combination while the tendon is irritable. Activity modification and load management are part of initial care [r8].

physio.name: Splinting or ulnar-side support
physio.description: A short period of splinting is a common first step and is in line with initial non-operative care in athletes [r8]. The splint design, position and duration are clinical choices without trial support.

physio.name: Progressive loading: ECU isometrics, then eccentric and isotonic loading, with kinetic-chain strengthening
physio.description: Strengthening components of the sport's kinetic chain is part of initial care [r8]. No randomised trial of a specific ECU loading program was retrieved; dosages in the rehab section are common clinical conventions.

physio.name: Forced passive stretching into supination, flexion and ulnar deviation, or heavy resisted ulnar deviation in that position
physio.description: This position tensions the ECU in the groove and predisposes to subluxation in cadavers [r13,r5]. Avoid provoking it repeatedly while the tendon or subsheath is irritable (clinical reasoning).

education: The ECU tendon runs in a groove on the little-finger side of the wrist, held in place by a thin sheath. Overload irritates the tendon, and a forceful twist can let it slip out of the groove.
Many people improve with a period of protection, load changes and gradual strengthening, but the trial evidence is limited, and some need an injection or surgery [r8,r1].
An audible or palpable snap is common in people with no pain at all, so it does not always need treatment [r5].
Avoid repeating the painful twisting combination (palm up, wrist bent toward the little finger side) under load while it settles, and review grip and swing technique with your coach.
If pain persists or the tendon keeps slipping, you may need a scan or a surgical opinion, and the wrist's ulnar-side ligament (TFCC) should be checked too [r12].

rehab.overview: This program applies to non-operative care of ECU tendinopathy and mild or stable subluxation. After subsheath reconstruction, or combined TFCC and ECU surgery, the surgeon's protocol (immobilisation duration, rotation limits) overrides it. Trials of specific ECU rehabilitation are lacking, so the stages are criteria-based, and dosages are common clinical conventions. The aims are to settle irritability, restore pain-free forearm rotation and wrist motion, rebuild ECU, forearm and grip strength along the sport's kinetic chain [r8], then return to grip-dependent sport with equipment and technique changes.

stages.name: Protect & settle
goals: Keep the shoulder, elbow and fingers moving
precautions: Avoid combined supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation under load
Follow the splint position and any surgical restrictions
Refer if the tendon subluxates repeatedly or if the DRUJ is unstable

exercises.name: Splint wear schedule
exercises.dosage: Wear as prescribed during aggravating tasks and at night for about 2–4 weeks (a common convention)
exercises.cues: Check fit and skin; keep the forearm out of supination while irritable

exercises.name: Active finger, thumb, elbow and shoulder range
exercises.cues: Keep the wrist still and relaxed

exercises.name: Pain-free wrist flexion and extension in neutral rotation
exercises.cues: Forearm supported and in neutral; stay within a comfortable range

exercises.name: Submaximal pain-free grip with the wrist neutral
exercises.dosage: 10 × 5 s holds at low effort, daily

exercises.name: Activity pacing and equipment check
exercises.dosage: Short blocks with rests; check grip size and swing volume with the coach
exercises.cues: Reduce repetitions of the painful movement

progressionCriteria: Able to grip lightly without provoking pain

stages.name: Restore motion & early loading
goals: Restore pain-free forearm rotation and wrist range
precautions: Keep pain at 3/10 or less during loading and settled within 24 hours
Avoid end-range supination with flexion and ulnar deviation
Stop if snapping or giving way increases

exercises.name: Active pronation and supination, elbow at 90°, within the pain-free range
exercises.cues: Slow and controlled; avoid end-range supination early

exercises.name: Isometric ECU holds in neutral (resisted ulnar deviation, forearm pronated)

criteria: Pain-free daily tasks with full or near-full forearm rotation and wrist range
No snapping or subluxation with supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation
Grip strength at about 90% of the other side (a common clinical convention)
Negative or minimally painful ECU synergy test and resisted ulnar deviation
Tolerates graded sport-specific grip and swing loads without a flare
TFCC and DRUJ screened and managed if involved; surgical clearance after reconstruction
tests: Grip dynamometry compared with the other side
ECU synergy test and resisted ulnar deviation

prognosis: Prognosis was not quantified in controlled trials. Initial care is usually non-operative [r8], and acute cases often respond to immobilisation while refractory cases need surgery [r16]. In a retrospective series, ECU sheath injection gave over 90% relief in all 11 patients with an isolated positive synergy test, but only 5 stayed pain free, and 10 of 22 patients with coexisting intra-articular signs had recurrent symptoms [r6]. After subsheath reconstruction, short-term results were satisfactory in a series of 7, with one asymptomatic recurrence on ultrasound and two re-operations [r18]. In 11 patients with combined TFCC and ECU surgery, 10 were pain free at an average 18 months [r14]. Snapping alone is common without symptoms (6.6%) and may not progress [r5]. Recurrence data, long-term outcomes and natural history of tendinopathy were not retrieved.
prevention: Build forearm rotation, ECU and grip strength and kinetic-chain strength before increasing racquet, club or stick load [r8].
Increase swing and hitting volume gradually, particularly with heavier equipment (clinical).
Check grip size, racquet or club weight and technique; avoid repeated ground strikes (clinical).
Warm up the forearm and wrist before gripping sport (clinical; no trial evidence retrieved).
Manage coexisting TFCC or DRUJ problems, since ECU pathology is associated with foveal tears [r12].
clinicalPearls: Don't treat a snap on its own: 6.6% of 755 asymptomatic people had ECU snapping, and MRI instability grading did not relate to symptoms [r5,r2].
The synergy test moderately raises or lowers probability (sensitivity 73.7%, specificity 85.7% in 40 wrists); use it with palpation of the groove and the rest of the ulnar-side examination [r7].
Always screen the TFCC and DRUJ: ECU tenosynovitis was more common in foveal tears (43% versus 23%), and injection relief in patients with intra-articular signs often did not last [r12,r6].
Use dynamic ultrasound when instability is suspected, and treat MRI with care: a high central signal in the ECU can be normal [r15].
Avoid provoking the supination, flexion and ulnar deviation combination while the sheath is irritable, because it is the position of greatest tension and subluxation [r13].
Be honest about the evidence: no randomised trials were retrieved for splinting, injection or surgery, so decisions are shared and based on function and sport demands [r1,r8].

animation.title: How ECU tendinopathy and subluxation develop

forces.label: Impact load through the gripped wrist
Repeated swings: flexion, supination, ulnar deviation

captions.text: A golfer practises hundreds of swings with a firm grip.
At impact the wrist is flexed, the forearm supinated and the wrist ulnar deviated.
The ECU tendon is tense in its groove at the ulnar head.
Repeated swings rub the tendon against the groove and its sheath.
A hard ground strike can stretch or tear the subsheath, letting the tendon slip.
Zooming into the right wrist, viewed from the palm side.

actions.text: ECU tendon in the sixth compartment
ECU subsheath holds it in the groove
Subluxation: the tendon snaps out of the groove

captions.text: The ECU runs along the ulnar side of the wrist in its own compartment.
A separate sheath, the subsheath, holds the tendon in the groove at the ulnar head.
A forceful twist can tear the subsheath, and the tendon subluxates with a snap.
Pain is felt over the ulnar groove; a snap alone can also be painless.
With repeated overload the tendon and sheath become irritated.
Tendinopathy or tenosynovitis follows, with pain on resisted ulnar deviation.
Healthy tendon: aligned collagen and a smooth gliding surface in its groove.
Repeated friction irritates the cells and swells the matrix (a generic tendon model).
With continued load the matrix becomes disorganised and thickened.
Chronic change: degenerative matrix with fibrovascular tissue.
Graded loading helps the tendon adapt, but a torn subsheath may need surgical reconstruction.
